data.title: Choose the correct answer for each question.
data.description: Practise inversion after negative and restrictive expressions and emphatic auxiliary structures.
learningPoints: Use auxiliary-subject inversion after negative adverbials placed first.
Use structures such as never have I..., rarely do we... and only then did I....
Use not only... but also with inversion when fronted.
Use emphatic do/does/did in affirmative clauses.
Recognise when inversion is formal or rhetorical.
Keep auxiliary and main verb forms accurate.

sections.explain: When NEVER begins the clause, invert auxiliary and subject.

words.word: Never have I seen such a beautiful view.
Never I have seen such a beautiful view.
Never have I saw such a beautiful view.
Rarely do we get an opportunity like this.
Rarely we do get an opportunity like this.
Rarely do we gets an opportunity like this.

sections.explain: ONLY THEN at the front triggers inversion in the main clause.

words.word: Only then did I understand what had happened.
Only then I did understand what had happened.
Only then did I understood what had happened.

sections.explain: A fronted NOT UNTIL phrase triggers inversion in the main clause.

words.word: Not until midnight did they finally arrive.
Not until midnight they finally arrived.
Not until midnight did they finally arrived.

sections.explain: When NOT ONLY begins the clause, invert auxiliary and subject.

words.word: Not only did she apologise, but she also offered a refund.
Not only she apologised, but she also offered a refund.
Not only did she apologised, but she also offered a refund.

sections.explain: HARDLY at the beginning can trigger inversion, often with WHEN.

words.word: Hardly had I sat down when the phone rang.
Hardly I had sat down when the phone rang.
Hardly had I sit down when the phone rang.

sections.explain: Negative fronted phrases trigger inversion in formal English.

words.word: Under no circumstances should you open this door.
Under no circumstances you should open this door.
Under no circumstances should you to open this door.

sections.explain: DO/DOES/DID can add emphasis to an affirmative statement.

words.word: I do understand your concern.
I am understand your concern.
I do understood your concern.

sections.explain: DID + base verb can emphasise that something really happened.

words.word: She did try to contact you.
She did tried to contact you.
She was try to contact you.
Seldom has the company faced such a serious challenge.
Seldom the company has faced such a serious challenge.
Seldom has the company face such a serious challenge.
